questions.source: LC Biology HL 2023, Section C, Question 11 (b) (i)-(ii)
questions.stem: (b) Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow. Ash dieback is a serious disease of ash trees caused by the invasive pathogen Hymenoscyphus fraxineus, which originates in Asia and was brought to Europe in the early 1990s. Ash dieback was first detected in the Republic of Ireland in October 2012 on plants imported from continental Europe. The disease is now prevalent throughout most of the island of Ireland and is likely to cause the death of the majority of the ash trees over the next two decades. This will also have an effect on organisms that feed on ash (such as moths) and other animals along the food chain (such as birds, e.g. the robin). Teagasc, the Irish agriculture development authority, is aiming to establish a gene bank composed of genotypes of ash trees that are tolerant or resistant to the deadly pathogen with the future aim of producing planting stocks for forests and hedgerows in Ireland. (Adapted from Ash Dieback Disease, www.teagasc.ie) [Parts (iii)-(vi), on food chains, pyramids and predation, are omitted.]

parts.label: (i)
parts.text: Name the type of ecological relationship that exists between ash trees and the pathogen that causes ash dieback.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text: From the passage, or otherwise, state a way that ecologists could ensure the survival of ash trees in Ireland.

points.answer: Establish a gene bank of resistant (or tolerant) trees

parts.text: The human body can defend itself against viruses using two defence systems: the general defence system and the specific defence system. Give two ways in which the general defence system works to defend against viruses and two ways in which the specific defence system defends against viruses.

questions.source: SEC Sample Paper 2 (2027), Higher Level, Question 1 (b) (Irish version, translated)
questions.stem: (Translated from Irish.) The following experiment was carried out to investigate the effectiveness of a vaccine. Read the article and answer the questions that follow. 'An international, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial was carried out to find out whether the vaccine was effective. In total 43 448 people received injections: 21 720 of them with the vaccine and 21 728 with the placebo. People aged 16 years or over were randomly assigned and they received two doses, 21 days apart, of the placebo or the vaccine. Two doses of the vaccine gave 95% protection against the pathogen in people aged 16 years or over.' (Adapted from Polack et al., 2020.)

parts.label: (i)
parts.text: Why was it important to test the vaccine on people from all over the world?

points.answer: People in different regions differ genetically (different ethnic backgrounds) and may respond differently to the vaccine
so the sample is representative of the global population / results apply worldwide (valid)
different strains/variants of the pathogen or different environments in different countries

parts.scheme_note: Unofficial answer.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text: What is meant by 'placebo-controlled' in the context of this experiment?

points.answer: A control group was given a placebo: an injection identical in appearance but with no vaccine (no active ingredient)
so the results of the vaccinated group can be compared with an unvaccinated group / any difference is due to the vaccine only (rules out the placebo effect)

parts.rule: likely one or two points (no official scheme)
parts.scheme_note: Unofficial answer.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.text: In total, 43 448 people aged 16 years or over took part in this experiment. Comment on the number of people in the sample used in this experiment in terms of the reliability of the data.

points.answer: A large sample size increases the reliability of the data
because it reduces the effect of chance / individual variation / anomalous results (results more representative and repeatable)

parts.rule: likely one or two points (no official scheme)
parts.scheme_note: Unofficial answer.

parts.label: (iv)
parts.text: Should the conclusion be drawn that this vaccine works on children under 16 years of age? Justify your answer.

points.answer: Only people aged 16 or over were tested, so the data cannot be extrapolated to children (children's immune systems may respond differently); a separate trial on under-16s would be needed

parts.scheme_note: Unofficial answer.

questions.source: SEC Sample Paper 2 (2027), Higher Level, Question 1 (e) (Irish version, translated)
questions.stem: (Translated from Irish.) Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow. 'Transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (TSEs) are a family of neurodegenerative disorders of the central nervous system (CNS) which include scrapie in sheep, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) in cattle, and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) and variant CJD (vCJD) in humans (World Health Organisation, WHO, 2002). TSEs occur as a result of the misfolding of a particular protein, called a prion, which is normally found on nerve-cell membranes in the brain.' (Adapted from fsai.ie)

diagram.what: Two ribbon models side by side: a normal protein (labelled 'Próitéin normálta', mostly coiled alpha-helices) and a prion (labelled 'Prión', the same chain refolded mostly into flat beta-sheet arrows).

labels.Prión: prion (misfolded form of the same protein)

parts.label: (i)
parts.text: Explain why prions can be classified as pathogens.

points.answer: they are infectious / transmissible: a prion causes normal proteins to misfold into prions

parts.rule: likely one or two points (no official scheme)
parts.scheme_note: Unofficial answer.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text: BSE was first identified in cattle in the United Kingdom in the 1980s, and the first cases of variant CJD were reported in 1996. Suggest a way in which this prion could be transmitted from cattle to humans, causing disease.

points.answer: Eating beef or beef products from infected cattle (especially nervous tissue: brain or spinal cord)

parts.scheme_note: Unofficial answer.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.text: Prions are an example of misfolded proteins. Explain the importance of folding in proteins.

points.answer: Folding gives the protein its specific 3D shape
the shape determines the protein's function (e.g. an enzyme's active site, a receptor's binding site); a misfolded protein cannot function / may cause disease

parts.scheme_note: Unofficial answer.

parts.label: (iv)

parts.scheme_note: Unofficial answer.

not_covered: Protists and parasitic animals as pathogens (e.g. Plasmodium/malaria, tapeworms, nematodes) (2.4.12).
Fungi as pathogens of humans or animals in a disease/immunity context (e.g. athlete's foot, ringworm); only a plant fungal pathogen (ash dieback, 2023-Q11b) appears (2.4.12).
Natural killer (NK) cells and their role (2.4.14).
B and T lymphocyte roles in the cell-mediated response as distinct from the antibody (humoral) response (2.4.12).
Differences between DNA and RNA viruses (e.g. RNA viruses mutate faster; retroviruses such as HIV use reverse transcriptase; examples of each) - only 'a virus contains DNA or RNA' is asked (2.4.13).
Reproduction number R0 (R value) and what it tells us about spread (2.4.15).
Persistence of a pathogen in a host (latent or chronic infection, carriers) as a factor in spread (2.4.15).
Chemical resistance other than antibiotic resistance (e.g. pesticide, fungicide or antiviral resistance) (2.4.15).
Local, regional and global movement of organisms/people as a factor in spread - appears only in passages (Zika and the Olympics, imported ash plants), never asked directly (2.4.15).
Novel viruses in plants and animals (emergence of a new virus, zoonotic spill-over) and why knowledge of emerging diseases matters to society (2.4.16).
Autoimmune diseases (e.g. type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis) (2.4.16).
Strategies to control an emerging disease beyond vaccination, antibiotics and Zika precautions (surveillance, isolation/quarantine, contact tracing, vector control) (2.4.16).
Treating microbial disease with antivirals or antifungals (2.4.12).
